title: Protest of Vistra Corp. regarding PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s proposed Interim Resource Adequacy Service filing under ER26-3515.

documents.name: Protest of Vistra Corp. - ER26-3515-000.pdf
documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                  BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


                                                            )
 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                                )           Docket No. ER26-3515-000
                                                            )



                                    PROTEST OF VISTRA CORP.

          Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“Commission”), 1 Vistra Corp. (“Vistra”) submits this protest regarding

PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) proposed Interim Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”)

proposal. Although Vistra recognizes PJM’s concerns regarding the resource adequacy challenges

facing the region, those concerns demand durable solutions that provide investors with the

certainty they need to maintain and expand PJM’s generation fleet.2 That is not IRAS.

          IRAS is ill-conceived, inconsistent with the Federal Power Act (“FPA”), and will stymie

investment in PJM. With IRAS, PJM ignores the jurisdictional boundaries that Congress carefully

crafted and proposes rules that are unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory—each of

which is a sufficient basis for the Commission to reject the proposal and for a court to overturn an

order accepting IRAS on appeal. In rejecting IRAS, the Commission should order PJM to develop

a durable solution that is faithful to sound market fundamentals to ensure that the region has the

capacity resources needed to meet load growth.




    1
        18 C.F.R. § 385.211.
    2
     For instance, the Commission’s proposed measures to incentivize load flexibility could provide the types of
durable solutions that bolster investor confidence, rather than undermine it. See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 195
FERC ¶ 61,211, at PP 85-87 (2026).
              Accepting IRAS would undermine the investor confidence that is critical to resource

     development because it would upset contracts negotiated in reliance on the rules in effect at the

     time. That is a particularly concerning result now, in PJM, where the absence of predictable market

     rules in recent years has significantly undermined investment in the generation fleet needed to

     maintain resource adequacy. If the Commission now casts doubt on the extent to which market

     participants, including both generation and load, can rely on already-executed or in-process

     bilateral contracts, it will only further impair PJM’s ability to meet its resource adequacy

     requirements at a time when the region can least afford it.3 To avoid that outcome, the Commission

     should reject IRAS altogether or clarify that new large loads that enter into contracts with existing

     capacity resources before the effective date of the IRAS reforms will not be subject to IRAS

     curtailments.

I.       PROTEST

             IRAS is both unlawful and counterproductive for the PJM region and the nation. It will

     hinder investment in generation resources and data infrastructure unless and until the Commission

     rejects the proposal. As explained below, IRAS runs afoul of the FPA in three distinct ways.

             First, as a threshold matter, IRAS oversteps the FPA’s jurisdictional boundaries because it

     targets retail customers that are outside of the Commission’s jurisdiction. Under IRAS, PJM will

     make wholesale curtailment decisions based entirely on whether an Electric Distribution Company

     (“EDC”) has certain specific retail customers (i.e., new large loads that do utilize the Bring Your

     no appetite to compromise investor confidence when those investors are driving the buildout of the generation that

 Own New Capacity (“BYONC”) pathway) in its footprint. That cuts directly against Congress’s

directive that retail service be regulated by the states, not by FERC.

         Second, IRAS is unduly discriminatory or preferential in multiple ways.4 Most glaringly,

IRAS and BYONC unduly discriminate against existing capacity resources. PJM proposes that

new large loads that contract with new capacity resources are not supposed to be exposed to the

IRAS curtailment regime while new large loads that contract with otherwise identical existing

capacity resources would be. This is textbook undue discrimination, as one MW of capacity from

a new resource provides the exact same resource adequacy benefits as one MW of capacity from

an otherwise identical existing resource. 5 After all, electrons don’t differ based on the age of the

generation facility that produced them. 6 To the extent proponents of IRAS assert that these MWs

are not identical because PJM needs one new MW of capacity for every new MW of load to solve

its resource adequacy concerns, they are wrong for two reasons. For one, they have not actually

demonstrated that the system cannot handle near-term load growth—and there are good reasons to

with the Commission under § 205 bears the burden of proving the adjustment is lawful.”); ISO New England Inc., 136
FERC ¶ 61,221, at P 20 (2011) (“Where . . . a filing is made under section 205 of the FPA, the burden of proof is on
the filing party to show that its proposal is just and reasonable.” (footnote omitted)).

efficient capacity are necessary to ensure reliability and both should receive the same price so that the price signals
are not skewed in favor of new entry.”); see also Calpine Corp., 171 FERC ¶ 61,034 (2020) (Glick, Comm’r,
Dissenting at P 84) (“[A] megawatt of capacity provided by a new resource is every bit as effective as a megawatt
provided by an existing one.”).
    6
       To underscore this point, consider how generators impact the system as a matter of physics. Electric energy is
“transmitted through the propagation of an electromagnetic wave;” electrons themselves do not “flow” but rather
“oscillate in place.” North Dakota v. Heydinger, 825 F.3d 912, 924 (8th Cir. 2016) (Murphy, J., concurring in part
and concurring in the judgment); see also Brief of Amicus Curiae of Electrical Engineers et al., New York v. FERC,
535 U.S. 1 (2002) (No. 00-568), 2001 WL 605124, at *7-8 (“The real energy transmission is accomplished through
the propagation of an electromagnetic wave. Each electron is induced, under the effect of the electromagnetic wave
generated at the power plant, to repel the electron in the next atom. Assume that energy is being transmitted left to
right in a wire. Each electron repels its right-hand neighbor, because they are both negatively charged and similar
charges repel each other. This ripple effect can be envisioned as each electron elbowing its neighbor toward the next
right-hand neighboring electron, which in turn elbows the next electron, and so on down the power line. The electrons
move very little, merely oscillating in place, but the energy – the electromagnetic wave – moves at the speed of light.
The energized electrons making the lightbulb in a house glow are not the same electrons that were induced to oscillate
in the generator at the generating plant.” (footnote omitted)).

                                                              -3-
 think that the system can, in fact, handle that load growth. 7 For the other, they misdiagnose the

problem: current resource adequacy concerns are caused by Load Serving Entities failing to

procure enough capacity to cover the entirety of their load obligation, not the contracting decisions

of individual retail customers. And they ignore the fact that IRAS represents an unprecedented

sea change in how customers’ service requests are viewed from a regulatory perspective. Vistra

is aware of no power market in history that has imposed a policy that says new customers are not

eligible for the same service as existing customers unless they procure their own generation

resources.8

         Third, IRAS has not been shown to be just and reasonable in several more respects. For

example, there is no assurance that new large loads will receive the purported benefit of BYONC

because it is up to states and EDCs to decide curtailment orders and priorities.9 Thus, IRAS would

impose a burden (BYONC) without any assurance that those bearing that burden would receive

the purported benefits that are supposed to flow from it (firm service). For that reason, IRAS is

an illusory construct that is fundamentally unjust and unreasonable. Further, IRAS violates cost

causation principles, and is therefore unjust and unreasonable, because it allocates capacity costs

to new large loads that do not bring new capacity even though it does not procure capacity to serve

those loads. It is also unjust and unreasonable because new large loads that do not bring new

which loads should ultimately reduce subject to IRAS.”).

demand response resources volunteer to be curtailed and are compensated as a result. Finally,

IRAS is unjust and unreasonable because, by removing from the Variable Resource Reliability

(“VRR”) Curve new large loads that do not bring new capacity, it would undermine capacity

market fundamentals, thereby further eroding resource adequacy in PJM.

           A. IRAS Violates the FPA’s Division of Jurisdiction

           The Commission is a creature of statute and can act only within the scope of authority

conveyed by Congress.10 IRAS exceeds the scope of the authority conveyed to the Commission

under the FPA because the entire scheme is based on and triggered by the characteristics and

behavior of retail customers (i.e., new large loads), which are within the states’ exclusive sphere

to regulate. In this way, IRAS explicitly “aims” at or “target[s]” specific retail customers, in

violation of the FPA.11

           The FPA gives the states exclusive authority over retail sales.12 This means that the

Commission is prohibited from specifying the rates, terms, and conditions of retail sales “no matter

how direct, or dramatic, [their] impact on wholesale rates” as that “is a job for the States alone.” 13

Nevertheless, “[w]holesale and retail markets in electricity . . . are not hermetically sealed from

each other,” so to determine whether an action that affects both wholesale and retail spheres

oversteps the FPA’s bright jurisdictional line, the Supreme Court has considered “the target at

    11

373, 385 (2015) (“Oneok”))).
    12
       16 U.S.C. § 824(b); Niagara Mohawk Power Corp. v. FERC, 452 F.3d 822, 824 (D.C. Cir. 2006) (“Under
section 201(b)(1) of the Federal Power Act, 16 U.S.C. § 824(b)(1), FERC has jurisdiction over both the interstate
transmission of electricity and the sale of electricity at wholesale in interstate commerce. States retain jurisdiction
over retail sales of electricity and over local distribution facilities.”).

which [the proposal] aims.” 15

           That is IRAS to a T. Under IRAS, PJM decides which wholesale transmission customers

are subject to curtailment based on the characteristics of individual retail customers—that is the

central feature of IRAS.16 Specifically, PJM will curtail EDCs with new large loads (i.e., retail

customers) in their footprints that do not bring sufficient new capacity to offset their demand.17

That makes IRAS all about the retail customer: when it comes online (before or after June 1, 2027),

its size (more or less than 50 MW), and whether it brings offsetting new capacity (i.e., BYONC).18

Under IRAS, retail customers and their characteristics are far more than “the mechanism through

which [IRAS] operates,” 19 they are lynchpin of the entire scheme and the determining factor for

whether IRAS applies. Moreover, PJM is clear, again and again, that the purpose of IRAS is to

shape the behavior of retail customers and to “solve” the resource adequacy challenge that PJM

posits, a task that should be reserved for the PJM capacity market.20

            Contrast IRAS with the Supreme Court’s decision in EPSA, where the Court upheld Order

No. 745 because (i) it did not literally regulate retail rates and (ii) the regulation did not target the

retail customer. 21 There, the demand response rule was “only about[] improving the wholesale

market,” and FERC “focused wholly on the benefits that demand response participation (in the

wholesale market) could bring to the wholesale market.”22 Any effects on the retail market were

incidental at most and beside the point. The same cannot be said of IRAS, which, as noted, is all

about specific retail loads and tailoring wholesale services to address the decisions and actions of

those retail loads. Whereas EPSA upheld a FERC decision that accommodated retail customers

by requiring RTOs/ISOs to enable them—if permitted by their state—to participate in FERC-

jurisdictional wholesale markets through a FERC-jurisdictional product, IRAS would, through

EDCs, regulate the nature and conditions of service that retail customers receive.

           It is obvious from how IRAS operates that PJM is targeting retail customers. Recall that

PJM proposes to assign wholesale curtailment obligation to an EDC based on the size (i.e., more

than 50 MW) and vintage (i.e., interconnection date and ramp rate) of the relevant retail

customers.23 PJM’s characterization of IRAS confirms the target, despite its veneer of regulating

EDCs rather than retail load. First, the PJM board directed PJM to file a proposal that “will be

applicable to ‘[N]ew Large Loads that, as of June 1, 2027, do not bring sufficient capacity to serve

their resource adequacy needs and cannot otherwise be served at the 1 -in-10 reliability

adequacy needs and avoid imposing costs on ratepayers.”).

customer—or that the curtailment directive is pursuant to a FERC-jurisdictional tariff. Indeed,

on the wholesale market and governs exclusively that market’s rules.”28

“‘exclusive jurisdiction’ rests with the states to ensure that the appropriate retail customers, i.e.,

           IRAS also exceeds the Commission’s authority for the related reason that PJM seeks to

regulate retail customers and their rates—albeit indirectly—which the FPA and EPSA prohibit. It

bears repeating that the Commission cannot regulate retail customers, even indirectly, in ways that

should be curtailed is a condition of retail distribution service, not something to be decided by an

RTO, as PJM would be doing here.

           PJM also proposes to overstep its jurisdictional limits by setting forth how retail customers

are compensated when they are curtailed under IRAS. 32 Under IRAS, PJM would compensate

EDCs for IRAS curtailments at a rate that is equal to 50% of the Non-Performance Charge Rate. 33

          Thus, IRAS regulates the retail customer, which is why it differs from other issues

involving large loads that lie at the confluence of federal and state jurisdiction. For example, in

           B. IRAS Is Unduly Discriminatory

           IRAS is also unduly discriminatory because it treats similarly situated entities differently.38

“Similarly situated” does not mean that there are no differences between the two entities, but rather

that there are no differences “that are material to the inquiry at hand.”39 PJM bears the burden to

explain how its proposal to treat entities differently is justified by factors that render those entities

not “similarly situated.” PJM fails to meet that standard for several reasons.

                     1. IRAS Unduly Discriminates Between EDCs

           To start, IRAS would unduly discriminate among EDCs based on the characteristics of

retail customers within those EDCs’ footprints. Specifically, IRAS would subject EDCs to

curtailment based on the size, timing, and contracting decisions of its retail customers. Those retail

customers are outside the Commission’s jurisdiction to consider and therefore cannot be “material

to the inquiry at hand.”40 Providing differing levels of wholesale market treatment depending on

legally irrelevant characteristics of entities sitting outside the Commission’s jurisdiction is, by

definition, unduly discriminatory.

           Even if the characteristics of the retail customers within an EDC’s territory could, in theory,

be a lawful basis to discriminate among wholesale customers, the retail characteristics on which

solve, and therefore do not render the EDCs differently situated. PJM has misdiagnosed the cause

of the resource adequacy problem. The regional resource adequacy problem is not caused by the

individual contracting decisions of each retail customer. The resource adequacy problem is that

some EDCs have agreed to serve more load than they have generation. Were PJM to continue to

assign load shed to EDCs that are short, it is likely that EDCs that interconnect large loads without

the generation to serve it would be exposed to curtailment. The current method aims at generation

deficient zones, with the potential they are short due to additional large loads. PJM skips past the

question of whether an EDC is generation deficient and aims simply at EDCs that have large loads

that do not bring their own new capacity.

                 2. IRAS Unduly Discriminates Against Existing Resources

       When determining whether new large loads are subject to IRAS, PJM would value identical

new and existing capacity resources differently even though they provide the same resource

adequacy benefits to the system. PJM has not explained why large loads that contract with new

generation resources should be non-curtailable while those that contract with existing generation

resource with the same capacity value should be curtailed when system conditions warrant. Nor

could it. One MW of accredited capacity from a new resource provides the same resource

adequacy benefits as one MW of capacity from an otherwise identical existing resource. Whether

the otherwise identical resources are bilaterally contracted or selling exclusively in the PJM

capacity market does not change the resource adequacy value to the PJM system as a matter of

physics.

       Indeed, the D.C. Circuit has held that is arbitrary and capricious for the Commission to

treat new and existing customers differently where both contribute equally to the need in



                                                    -12-
 question.41 So too, the Commission has previously rejected efforts by PJM to treat new and

existing capacity resources differently, even when the avowed purpose was to incentivize new

resource entry.42 In that case, PJM proposed to lock in capacity prices for new capacity resources

for seven years, which would guarantee higher prices to new entrants that were not available to

existing suppliers. The Commission rejected the proposal, explaining that both new and existing

capacity are necessary to ensure reliability and that both should receive the same price so that the

price signals are not skewed in favor of new entry.43 That logic applies with force here because

IRAS gives preferential treatment to one MW of new capacity even though one MW of existing

capacity is equally as effective when it comes to ensuring resource adequacy.

                    3. IRAS Unduly Discriminates Based on Vintage of Load Addition

          Next, IRAS also unduly discriminates between new and existing large loads given that

curtailment obligations would be assigned to the EDC based on when the large loads in question

began operating, a characteristic that is entirely irrelevant to reliability and resource adequacy

concerns. As already discussed, the D.C. Circuit has rejected similar efforts to treat existing and

marginal customers differently based on the principal that, because every user of a system is

economically marginal, increases in demand can be attributed to every user, both new and

existing.44 That principle forecloses IRAS, which would treat EDCs with large loads that begin

operations on May 31, 2027 differently than those with large loads that begin operations the next

           PJM’s proposal to reset the IRAS curtailment regime if the region has sufficient capacity

to meet the reliability requirement for three consecutive delivery years further underscores the

curtailments going forward even if a shortfall returns in year six.45 But a new load coming online

scheme in this way makes no sense, as the demand that the large load puts on PJM’s system (i.e.,

picture in PJM at the time those loads begin operating rather than on the loads’ effects on resource

adequacy—a principle that is inconsistent with the D.C. Circuit’s BNP Paribas decision.46

new large loads to bring new capacity to avoid being curtailed even though PJM lacks the authority

to ensure that such loads will not, in fact, be curtailed. Second, under IRAS, new large loads that

do not bring new capacity are allocated costs for capacity that PJM never procures. Third, IRAS
